summary: Prescription melatonin-receptor agonist for circadian rhythm sleep disorders (Non-24 and Smith-Magenis–related nighttime sleep disturbance). Taken nightly, but results can take weeks to show up.
description: Hetlioz is a circadian “reset” medication, not a quick knockout sleep pill. It’s used for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder (especially in totally blind patients) and for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith-Magenis syndrome. You take it every night at the same time, about an hour before bed—then you give it time. Some people notice changes in sleep over weeks; for others it can take months. Biggest watch-outs: next-day grogginess, weird dreams, and drug interactions that can tank effectiveness or increase side effects. Capsules and the liquid (Hetlioz LQ) are not interchangeable mg-for-mg.
patient_summary: Hetlioz is for circadian rhythm sleep problems—not a fast “sleep now” med. Take it every night at the same time, 1 hour before bed, and be patient: it may take weeks (sometimes longer) to see the full effect. Common issues are headache, unusual dreams/nightmares, and infections like URIs/UTIs. Avoid alcohol, and make sure your prescriber checks for drug interactions. Capsules and the liquid are NOT interchangeable.

primary.context: FDA-approved for Non-24. Efficacy was established in totally blind patients. It’s meant to help entrain (re-align) the sleep-wake cycle over time—not provide immediate sedation.
FDA-approved (by age/formulation) for nighttime sleep disturbances associated with Smith-Magenis syndrome. Taken nightly, consistently, to support more stable sleep timing.

secondary.context: This is not a general insomnia medication. It’s specifically used when insomnia is driven by circadian rhythm misalignment (timing problem), not just difficulty falling asleep for any reason.

therapeutic_response.display: Clinical effect may take weeks or months due to circadian rhythm differences

common_adverse_effects.notes: If headaches are frequent or severe, hydration and sleep timing help—but also tell your prescriber. Persistent headaches can be a reason to reassess dosing timing or whether the med is a fit.
This doesn’t always mean liver injury, but it’s a signal to monitor. If you develop jaundice, dark urine, severe fatigue, or right-upper-abdominal pain—get checked urgently.
Vivid dreams can be tolerable—or they can mess with sleep and mood. If nightmares are frequent, distressing, or trigger daytime anxiety, bring it up.
Usually mild, but if you have fever, shortness of breath, or symptoms that drag on, treat it like a real illness—not a side effect you ignore.
Burning with urination, urgency, pelvic pain—don’t wait it out. UTIs are treatable, and ignoring them can make things worse.

serious_risks.risk: Severe sedation or impaired alertness leading to accidents (higher risk if combined with alcohol or other sedatives)
Clinically significant liver issues (rare, but watch for jaundice, dark urine, severe fatigue, abdominal pain)
Hypersensitivity reactions to excipients in certain formulations (rare; risk depends on individual sensitivity)

contraindications.contraindication: There are no contraindications listed in the manufacturer’s labeling.

precautions: CNS depression: Can impair physical and mental abilities (think: driving, machinery, decisions)
Severe liver disease: Use is not recommended (has not been studied)
Older adults: Higher exposure may increase side effects—use caution
Smokers: Exposure is lower in smokers, which can reduce effectiveness
Alcohol: Avoid or limit ethanol—combining sedatives is never a flex

interactions.mechanism: Worsened CNS depression, impaired coordination and judgment, poorer sleep quality, higher accident risk.
interactions.action: Avoid or strictly limit alcohol. If you drink, don’t take this as a “sleep chaser.”

interactions.interactant: Strong CYP1A2 or CYP3A4 inhibitors (interaction risk)
interactions.mechanism: Higher tasimelteon exposure may increase sedation, next-day impairment, and adverse effects.
interactions.action: Review all meds and supplements with your prescriber/pharmacist. Dose adjustment or avoidance may be needed depending on the interacting drug.

interactions.interactant: Strong CYP1A2 or CYP3A4 inducers (interaction risk)
interactions.mechanism: Lower tasimelteon exposure can reduce efficacy (basically: you’re taking it, but it may not land).
interactions.action: Avoid inducing agents when possible or reassess whether this medication is worth continuing under those conditions.

interactions.mechanism: Exposure is decreased in smokers compared with nonsmokers, which can reduce efficacy.
interactions.action: If you smoke and Hetlioz isn’t working, this may be part of why. Tell your prescriber—don’t just assume the med is useless.

interactions.interactant: Other sedating medications (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, sleep aids, cannabis, etc.)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation and impairment. Higher fall/accident risk.
interactions.action: Use caution, especially early in treatment. Avoid stacking sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly planned it.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Sleep timing and drift: Track bedtime, wake time, naps, and nighttime awakenings (sleep diary is the simplest high-yield tool)
Daytime impairment: Next-day grogginess, slowed thinking, reaction time changes—especially early on and in older adults
Dream changes: Vivid dreams/nightmares that disrupt sleep or worsen daytime anxiety/mood
Medication timing consistency: Same time nightly is essential; inconsistent timing can look like “it doesn’t work”
Drug interaction review: New meds, antibiotics, antifungals, supplements, and smoking changes can all shift exposure
Alcohol and sedative stacking: Screen for alcohol use and concurrent sedating meds that increase impairment risk
Liver labs if clinically indicated: Especially if there’s pre-existing liver disease, symptoms of liver dysfunction, or unexplained fatigue/jaundice
Infection symptoms: URI/UTI symptoms when they appear—don’t just assume it’s “nothing”

special_populations.pregnancy: Adverse events were observed in animal reproduction studies. In humans, use during pregnancy should be a risk-benefit decision focused on symptom severity, alternatives, and functional risk from untreated sleep-wake disorder.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if tasimelteon is excreted into breast milk. The manufacturer recommends weighing infant exposure risk, benefits of breastfeeding, and benefits of treatment to the mother.
special_populations.pediatric: Smith-Magenis syndrome nighttime sleep disturbances: Children ≥3 years and adolescents <16 years use the oral suspension dosing based on weight (≤28 kg: 0.7 mg/kg once nightly 1 hour before bed; >28 kg: 20 mg once nightly 1 hour before bed). Adolescents ≥16 years use the 20 mg capsule once nightly 1 hour before bed. Capsules vs suspension are not interchangeable mg-for-mg.
special_populations.geriatric: Use with caution. In older adults, exposure can be increased (about two-fold compared with younger adults), which may raise the chance of next-day impairment and other adverse events.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Adults: no dosage adjustment necessary. Pediatric renal impairment: no specific guidance in labeling; based on adult data, adjustment is likely unnecessary.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment necessary. Severe hepatic impairment: use is not recommended (not studied).

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Capsule: absorption reduced and time-to-peak delayed with a high-fat meal
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Fasting: capsule ~0.5 to 3 hours; oral suspension ~15 to 30 minutes
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP1A2 and CYP3A4; phase II glucuronidation
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High-fat meal delays Tmax and reduces peak levels (capsule); administer without food

dosing.titration: This is a nightly circadian routine medication. Dose timing matters as much as the dose itself: take it 1 hour before bedtime, at the same time every night. Don’t take it with food. If you can’t take it around your usual time on a given night, skip the dose—don’t double up. Capsules and the oral suspension are not interchangeable.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Hetlioz is not a benzodiazepine and is not known for a classic dangerous withdrawal syndrome. Most people can stop it without a formal taper. The main “rebound” risk is your circadian sleep problem returning—sometimes quickly—because the medication’s benefit depends on consistent, ongoing rhythm support.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Hetlioz is a circadian rhythm medication used when the core problem is sleep timing—your internal clock is out of sync. It’s not for everyday insomnia. It’s for Non-24 (most established in totally blind patients) and for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith-Magenis syndrome.
items: {link:condition:non-24-hour-sleep-wake-disorder:Non-24-hour Sleep-Wake Disorder (Non-24)}: Your sleep schedule drifts later (or sometimes earlier) day by day because your body clock won’t lock onto a 24-hour day
{link:condition:smith-magenis-syndrome:Smith-Magenis Syndrome (SMS)} nighttime sleep disturbances: Chronic sleep disruption tied to circadian rhythm differences in SMS

sections.heading: What People Feel

No instant magic. I had to stop expecting a quick sleep pill effect.
The main change early on was making bedtime feel more structured.

Fewer nights of being wide awake at a random hour.

items.note: For circadian meds, consistency is the whole game. Same time, every night.

quotes: Nightmares popped up more than usual.

items.note: Abnormal dreams/nightmares are reported. If it’s unbearable or affecting daytime mood, tell your prescriber.

quotes: A little groggy in the morning at first.

items.note: After taking it, keep activities limited to getting ready for sleep. Avoid alcohol.

sections.intro: This med is a slow-burn. Most people don’t feel a dramatic “hit” the first night. What they notice (if it’s working) is their sleep pattern getting less chaotic over time.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Hetlioz can start changing circadian timing early, but the meaningful, real-life sleep improvements can take weeks—or even months—depending on your baseline rhythm and how consistent you are with dosing.
key_points: Not a rapid sedative: You may not feel an immediate “sleepy” effect
Weeks to months: Full circadian benefit can take time (individual rhythms vary a lot)
Take 1 hour before bedtime: Then keep your night low-stimulation and sleep-focused
Short blood half-life (~1–2 hours): But the clinical goal is rhythm alignment over time, not all-night sedation
Food matters (capsule): High-fat meals can delay peak levels and reduce the peak effect—take without food

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Hetlioz is most effective when the sleep problem is truly circadian—meaning your internal clock is drifting or mis-timed. In Non-24, the best-studied benefit is helping the sleep-wake cycle lock onto a 24-hour day over time (especially in totally blind patients). In Smith-Magenis syndrome, the goal is fewer nighttime disruptions and a more stable night sleep pattern. If you’re expecting a same-night rescue effect, it will disappoint you. If you treat it like a nightly circadian routine, it has a real chance to help.
sections.metric: Circadian realignment (entrainment) and improved sleep timing
sections.clinical_details: Response is not immediate. This medication is taken nightly at the same time, and clinicians often use sleep logs (and sometimes circadian markers) to judge whether the sleep window is stabilizing over weeks. Missed timing, inconsistent dosing, interacting meds, and smoking-related metabolism changes can all reduce the chance of benefit.

sections.intro: Tasimelteon is metabolized primarily by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4. Some interacting meds can meaningfully change exposure—either increasing side effects or making the medication less effective. This is one of those meds where “check interactions” is not optional.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Hetlioz is not a benzodiazepine and is not known for a classic dangerous withdrawal syndrome. Most people can stop it without a formal taper. The main “rebound” risk is your circadian sleep problem returning—sometimes quickly—because the medication’s benefit depends on consistent, ongoing rhythm support.
key_points: No standard taper required for most patients
If you stop, your sleep-wake rhythm can drift again (especially in Non-24)
If side effects are an issue, discuss timing, interactions, and formulation before quitting
If you’re on multiple sedating meds, your prescriber may still recommend a stepwise plan just to track what’s causing what

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: This is a nightly circadian routine medication. Dose timing matters as much as the dose itself: take it 1 hour before bedtime, at the same time every night. Don’t take it with food. If you can’t take it around your usual time on a given night, skip the dose—don’t double up. Capsules and the oral suspension are not interchangeable.

adult.non24_bedtime: 20 mg PO once daily, taken 1 hour before bedtime; take at the same time each night
adult.smith_magenis_bedtime: 20 mg PO once daily, taken 1 hour before bedtime; take at the same time each night
adult.missed_dose: If the dose cannot be taken at approximately the same time on a given night, skip that dose (do not double the next dose)
adult.food_instruction: Administer without food (high-fat meals can delay Tmax and reduce peak levels for the capsule)
adult.formulation_interchangeability: Capsules and oral suspension are not interchangeable; do not switch forms without prescriber guidance
adult.renal_adjustment: No dosage adjustment necessary in adults
adult.hepatic_adjustment: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment necessary; severe impairment: use is not recommended (not studied)
adult.drug_interaction_note: Significant drug interactions exist; dose/frequency adjustment or avoidance may be needed depending on concomitant therapy

sections.simple_explanation: Think of this medication as a “body clock trainer,” not a fast sedative. Taking it at the same time nightly—and keeping your bedtime routine consistent—is what gives it a chance to work.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Data in pregnancy and breastfeeding are limited. The bigger real-world issues tend to be sedation/impairment risk (especially in older adults), reduced exposure in smokers, and formulation-specific excipients in the liquid product for younger patients.
sections.pregnancy: Adverse events were observed in animal reproduction studies. In humans, use during pregnancy should be a risk-benefit decision focused on symptom severity, alternatives, and functional risk from untreated sleep-wake disorder.
sections.lactation: It is not known if tasimelteon is excreted into breast milk. The manufacturer recommends weighing infant exposure risk, benefits of breastfeeding, and benefits of treatment to the mother.
sections.pediatrics: Smith-Magenis syndrome nighttime sleep disturbances: Children ≥3 years and adolescents <16 years use the oral suspension dosing based on weight (≤28 kg: 0.7 mg/kg once nightly 1 hour before bed; >28 kg: 20 mg once nightly 1 hour before bed). Adolescents ≥16 years use the 20 mg capsule once nightly 1 hour before bed. Capsules vs suspension are not interchangeable mg-for-mg.
sections.geriatrics: Use with caution. In older adults, exposure can be increased (about two-fold compared with younger adults), which may raise the chance of next-day impairment and other adverse events.
sections.hepatic: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment necessary. Severe hepatic impairment: use is not recommended (not studied).
sections.renal: Adults: no dosage adjustment necessary. Pediatric renal impairment: no specific guidance in labeling; based on adult data, adjustment is likely unnecessary.
sections.other_notes: Smokers may have decreased exposure (~40% lower), which can reduce efficacy. Some oral suspension products may contain excipients like sodium benzoate/polysorbate 80; use extra caution in neonates and medically fragile infants (the labeled pediatric indication starts at age 3).

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sleep timing and drift: Track bedtime, wake time, naps, and nighttime awakenings (sleep diary is the simplest high-yield tool)
Daytime impairment: Next-day grogginess, slowed thinking, reaction time changes—especially early on and in older adults
Dream changes: Vivid dreams/nightmares that disrupt sleep or worsen daytime anxiety/mood
Medication timing consistency: Same time nightly is essential; inconsistent timing can look like “it doesn’t work”
Drug interaction review: New meds, antibiotics, antifungals, supplements, and smoking changes can all shift exposure
Alcohol and sedative stacking: Screen for alcohol use and concurrent sedating meds that increase impairment risk
Liver labs if clinically indicated: Especially if there’s pre-existing liver disease, symptoms of liver dysfunction, or unexplained fatigue/jaundice
Infection symptoms: URI/UTI symptoms when they appear—don’t just assume it’s “nothing”

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Hetlioz comes as a capsule and as an oral suspension (Hetlioz LQ). They are not interchangeable mg-for-mg, so don’t switch forms without a prescriber’s direction.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Tasimelteon is an agonist at melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2 (with greater affinity for MT2). In plain English: it works on the same signaling system your brain uses to time sleep and circadian rhythms. MT1 activity is linked to sleepiness, while MT2 activity is more tied to shifting and stabilizing circadian timing—exactly what you’re trying to fix in Non-24 and Smith-Magenis–related sleep disruption.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Hetlioz is a specialist-style tool for circadian rhythm disorders. It’s most appropriate when the diagnosis is clear (Non-24, or Smith-Magenis nighttime sleep disturbance) and when the patient can commit to consistent nightly timing. For general insomnia, clinicians usually start elsewhere: sleep hygiene, CBT-I, and targeted treatment of anxiety/depression. Hetlioz is about aligning the clock—not sedating you into sleep.

faqs.q: Is Hetlioz a regular sleeping pill?
faqs.a: Not really. It’s not designed to knock you out quickly like some sedatives. Hetlioz is a circadian rhythm medication—meant to help your body clock align more predictably over time. If your problem is timing (Non-24, Smith-Magenis–related disruption), it can help. If your problem is general insomnia for other reasons, it’s usually not the first choice.

faqs.q: How long does Hetlioz take to work?
faqs.a: It can take weeks—and sometimes longer. That’s not a failure; that’s how circadian realignment works. The label specifically notes that effects may not occur for weeks or months because circadian rhythms vary person to person.

faqs.q: How do I take Hetlioz correctly?
faqs.a: Take it without food, 1 hour before bedtime, at the same time every night. After you take it, keep activities limited to preparing for sleep. If you can’t take it around your usual time one night, skip that dose—don’t double up the next night.

faqs.q: What conditions is Hetlioz approved to treat?
faqs.a: It’s used for Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder (with efficacy established in totally blind patients) and for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith-Magenis syndrome (age/formulation dependent).

faqs.q: Can I switch between Hetlioz capsules and Hetlioz LQ liquid?
faqs.a: Don’t do that casually. Capsules and oral suspension are not interchangeable on a mg-for-mg basis. If a switch is needed, it should be a prescriber-guided change.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Headache is the most common. People also report abnormal dreams or nightmares, and some get infections like URIs or UTIs. Lab-wise, liver enzymes (ALT) can increase in some patients, so symptoms of liver problems should be taken seriously.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with Hetlioz?
faqs.a: Avoid or limit alcohol. Alcohol can worsen sedation/impairment and can trash sleep quality. Mixing sedating substances is one of the fastest ways to create a safety problem.
Yes. Smoking induces CYP1A2 and is associated with lower tasimelteon exposure (about 40% lower in smokers), which can reduce effectiveness. If you smoke and it’s not working, tell your prescriber.

faqs.q: Is Hetlioz safe in liver disease?
faqs.a: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: no dosage adjustment is generally needed. Severe hepatic impairment: use is not recommended (not studied). If you have significant liver disease, your prescriber should weigh alternatives and monitor closely.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off Hetlioz?
faqs.a: Most people don’t. It’s not known for dangerous withdrawal like benzodiazepines. The main issue when stopping is the sleep-wake disorder returning because the benefit depends on consistent nightly support.

faqs.q: Why do I feel groggy the next day?
faqs.a: CNS depression is possible, especially early on, in older adults, or if you combine it with other sedating meds or alcohol. Also: if you take it and then stay up doing stimulating stuff, you may feel worse the next day. Take it, wind down, go to bed.
